title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Failed
dek: Phase-change memory went from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
why: A complete history of a storage technology's failure, from RMM in 1970 to the shutdown of Optane in 2022. Information density is moderate; the second half, on data-center deployment and Micron's exit, is the most valuable part.
who: Engineers and investors watching memory chips, data-center hardware and semiconductor industry history, especially those who want to understand why a new technology gets squeezed out by a cheaper old one.
skip: The first minute of technical background can be fast-forwarded; jump straight to the phase-change storage mechanism at 3:07.

points.h: The physics of phase-change memory makes it slow
points.body: Phase-change memory stores data by switching a material between crystalline and amorphous states: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and then cools it slowly to crystallize, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystal without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

points.h: Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot
points.body: In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Gordon Moore of Intel published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell had a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 micrometers, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later, when someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, he said he had no memory of it at all.

points.h: Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
points.body: The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into long-term decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with investment from Francisco Partners and bank loans. NOR lacked NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM—PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabits and 90 nanometers.

points.h: Mobile PCM was wiped out by a wave of 3D NAND
points.body: PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stored boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512-megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% in power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1-gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, removing mobile PCM's most compelling rationale. In January 2014 Micron announced it was withdrawing from mobile PCM.

points.h: Intel and Micron were split from the start on Optane's positioning
points.body: In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly split, each going independent after completing joint development of the second generation of 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs through volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance, or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel shifted to producing it itself.

points.h: Putting Optane in the data center required redoing motherboards and software
points.body: In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode combined Optane and DRAM into one volatile memory pool, worked out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price fluctuations; App Direct Mode was the truly valuable mode, letting software write persistent data to Optane so it survived a reboot. Oracle or SAP databases typically take more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives after a restart, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directional test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency issues.

points.h: Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the truly useful mode
points.body: In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata as the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not included in the deal, which looked like an endorsement but also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 exceeded $500 million.

points.h: After Micron's exit, Optane was left with a single supplier
points.body: In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged the company down by $400 million a year; the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to the continuing fall in 3D NAND prices and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron instead bet on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory—GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was proprietary technology. In July 2022 Intel quietly announced the shutdown of the Optane business on its earnings call.

terms.def: A non-volatile memory technology jointly announced by Intel and Micron in 2015, later made into Optane and QuantX respectively.
A non-volatile memory that stores data using the resistance difference between a material's crystalline and amorphous states.
A memory category between hard drives and solid-state storage, combining non-volatility with access speeds close to DRAM.
Optane's persistent memory mode, in which software can write persistent data directly to the Optane module.
An open-standard interface that connects compute, memory and storage systems into pools that can be allocated on demand.
